items.title: Emotional content can improve how people process conversations
items.summary: New in JNeurosci, Pyry Heikkinen and colleagues, from the University of Helsinki, explored how emotional meaning influences the way the human brain prioritizes information during naturally spoken conversations in a cocktail party setting.

items.title: Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona
items.summary: From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain.

items.title: World-famous or local legend? New study investigates global and local forms of collective memory and group identity
items.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte and Bernardo O'Higgins: two 19th-century military leaders renowned to this day in their native countries of France and Chile. items.title: Lizard tail preserved in amber sheds light on a 100-million-year-old defense mechanism
items.summary: A lizard making a dramatic escape, leaving its tail wriggling behind as it darts to safety, is an image familiar to many. items.title: Solving an ancient cold case: Roman was brutally murdered
items.summary: This 2,000-year-old cold case offered a wealth of information, Leiden archaeologists Carol van Driel-Murray and Mark Driessen explain. items.title: Britain's 1972 school reform may have lowered dementia diagnoses half a century later
items.summary: A new study provides perhaps the strongest evidence yet that education can help mitigate long-term dementia risk.

items.title: Japan's largest marine DNA study detects 126 fish species farther north than previously recorded
items.summary: As climate change reshapes habitats both on land and at sea, you might go to the beach one day, only to find yourself in a place that looks nothing like you remember, around sea creatures you don't recognize.

items.title: Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest
items.summary: Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. items.title: Physicists reveal new paradigm for fiber growth in neurodegenerative diseases
items.summary: Some proteins that are linked to neurodegenerative diseases can form both liquid droplets and amyloid fibers. But how are these two states connected, and where do the fibers grow? Leiden physicists Liru Feng and Louise Jawerth have discovered a counter-intuitive mechanism.

items.title: An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?
items.summary: A U.S. startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night.

items.title: Mapping the hidden global labor powering AI
items.summary: Most people know by now that artificial intelligence powers much of the online world, sifting through social media posts, planning driving routes or helping to choose a movie to watch. items.summary: NASA test pilot Mike Lippert poses for a photo ahead of his first time flying the agency’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026. items.title: Sediment core reveals volcanic eruption preceded ancient cold spell by about 150 years
items.summary: A new study led by an international research team including scientists at the University of South Carolina challenges the idea that the ancient Laacher See volcanic eruption in western Europe triggered a significant climate-cooling period affecting central Europe and the Arctic nearly 13,000 years a

items.title: While some eucalypts are hard to kill, climate change may test the ability of others to survive
items.summary: There's no tree like the humble eucalypt.

items.title: Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
items.summary: In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. items.title: Protein fibers, a hallmark of Alzheimer's, spotted making genetic deliveries to sperm cells
items.summary: Unexpectedly, a kind of protein that is usually linked with diseases in the brain may play a vital role in semen, helping shepherd genetic material into sperm cells, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute report in the journal Molecular Cell.

items.title: Plants may switch between reproductive strategies more easily than thought
items.summary: When it comes to reproduction, plants have options. Some can fertilize themselves, while others rely on pollen from genetically different plants. items.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
items.summary: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience.

items.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
items.summary: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment.

items.title: Diamond defects confirm 80-year-old theory of crystal stress
items.summary: For the first time, researchers in Japan have directly mapped several components of the stress field surrounding an atomic-scale flaw in the crystal structure of diamond. items.title: Tiny shifts in iron content tip a potential memory material between competing magnetic states
items.summary: A team of Yale researchers has figured out what gives a magnetic material its mysterious properties, a discovery that could help boost computing memory and the field of "spintronics." Their work is published in Physical Review Letters.

items.title: Thermal priming enhances heat tolerance and yield in tomatoes after recurrent heat stress
items.summary: High temperatures can significantly impair the growth and yield of crops, including tomatoes. items.title: An 'electron waiting room' helps blue titanium dioxide hold light energy longer
items.summary: To produce hydrogen using sunlight, the energy obtained from light must be retained until it can be used in a chemical reaction. However, if an electron that has gained energy from light quickly returns to its original position, it becomes difficult to make use of that energy.

items.title: Barley seed could carry fungicide-resistant disease into next crop, researchers find
items.summary: Barley seed could be carrying more than the potential for a new crop, with emerging research from the University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ) finding that fungicide-resistant net blotch can be carried on seed and transferred to seedlings.

items.title: Ahead of their time: Restricted to pre-2018 research, AI flags hydrogen catalyst reported in later experiments
items.summary: Researchers have used artificial intelligence to identify promising catalysts using only the scientific knowledge that was available years before their actual discovery. Their findings could accelerate the search for more efficient hydrogen production and other valuable chemical processes.

items.title: NASA, USDA Sign Agreement Advancing Earth Science, Agriculture

items.title: People may have preexisting immunity to bird flu
items.summary: How immune are people to bird flu viruses? To find out, Canadian virologists analyzed blood samples that 24 health care workers at Université de Montréal's teaching hospital, the CHUM, gave before and after getting their annual flu shot.

items.title: Znanstvenici: Testosteron bi mogao imati neočekivanu korist za žene nakon menopauze
items.summary: NOVO istraživanje pokazuje da dodavanje testosterona hormonskoj terapiji može učinkovitije zaštititi gustoću kostiju žena u postmenopauzi, posebno u kralježnici, u usporedbi sa samim estrogenom.

items.title: One extra quantum dot helps balance speed and stability in spin qubits
items.summary: Quantum computers need qubits that can be controlled both quickly and reliably. Yet making semiconductor spin qubits faster often makes them more sensitive to electrical noise, creating a difficult trade-off.

items.title: JWST and ALMA reveal a dusty, rapidly growing black hole in the early universe
items.summary: A new study reveals a dust-reddened quasar from a time when the universe was less than a billion years old. items.title: Can we really predict the future? Over one million forecasts offer clues, not certainty
items.summary: Can crowds of people trading on what they believe will happen collectively predict the future? A new Tel Aviv University study of more than 1 million forecasts suggests that they often come remarkably close. items.title: Researchers improve RNA extraction from precision-cut lung slices
items.summary: Precision-cut lung slices allow researchers to study living human lung tissue outside the body, preserving the different cell types and structures that make up the organ. But a material that helps scientists create these slices can also make it difficult to study the genetic activity within them.

items.title: Rain gardens offer a balanced solution for managing urban stormwater near Tokyo

items.title: Greenwashing fears may drive up the cost of climate finance
items.summary: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from industries such as steelmaking, chemicals and energy production requires enormous investment. items.title: New statewide lidar study identifies hot spots for California coastal cliff retreat
items.summary: The cliffs that comprise much of California's coastline are constantly being reshaped by rain, waves and other geologic forces. The erosion of cliffs threatens critical infrastructure such as highways, railways, homes, parklands, public access points and more.

items.title: Suicide attempts, ideation spiked significantly among older U.S. adults after COVID-19 pandemic
items.summary: New research from UCLA Health and UC San Diego Health found a significant spike in suicidal thoughts, planning and attempts among older U.S. adults in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic.

items.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
items.summary: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

items.summary: A new study demonstrates that embedding short, asynchronous mindfulness practices into Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) curricula effectively reduces stress, combats burnout, and builds essential leadership skills. items.summary: Astronomers have found a vast reservoir of hydrogen with something conspicuously missing: detectable starlight. items.summary: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. items.summary: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. items.summary: Teacher shortages are affecting school systems in countries across the world. Governments have responded with initiatives to attract graduates into teaching. items.title: Assessment tool helps schools look at students holistically
items.summary: Researchers in the Neag School of Education are bringing a whole child screening assessment to a company that provides schools with a connected set of solutions that turn every student signal into timely, equitable, coordinated and measurable tools to track and manage supports.

items.title: Australian coral reefs face risk of collapse within 50 years without drastic action, global assessment finds
items.summary: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment.

items.summary: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys. items.title: Storms batter Europe, hitting power supplies, flights and phones
items.summary: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks.

items.title: Monarchs report their locations via… cellphone?
items.summary: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey? That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram (0.02 ounces).

items.title: Milky Way's disk grew 'upside down,' with younger stars forming in ever-thinner layers
items.summary: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics. It's divided into a galactic bulge, a galactic disk and a galactic halo.

items.title: How screening tools measure disadvantage may leave rural communities overlooked for public support
